cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: Roman society was rigidly hierarchical with patricians at the top and slaves at the bottom

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: Patricians were the aristocratic families who held political power and owned vast estates

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: Plebeians were the common citizens — farmers, traders, artisans and labourers

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: The Conflict of the Orders gradually gave plebeians more political rights over centuries

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: The patron-client system bound lower-status Romans to elite patrons in exchange for support and protection

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: The paterfamilias had absolute legal authority (patria potestas) over his entire household

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: Slaves were property with no legal rights — they could be freed to become freedmen (liberti)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: Freedmen occupied an ambiguous social position — they were citizens but carried the stigma of former slavery

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: The equestrian order (equites) was a wealthy business class below the senatorial aristocracy

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: Roman women could not vote or hold office but managed households and could own property

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: Social mobility was limited but possible — freedmen's children were full citizens

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Social Structure
cards.back: The census classified citizens by wealth, determining their political rights and military obligations
